chapter_theme: Three songs at Tirupperunthurai (திருப்பெருந்துறை): the body as a house of blood and bone that sickens, bends and becomes a corpse; the embrace of women and the great sea of birth; the memory of a night's lovemaking that the poet asks to have erased. Murugan is praised as guru to his father, beside Siva seated as guru under the kurunda tree.
structure_note: 843 is a body-and-ageing song, 844 and 845 courtesan and lovemaking songs; 843 and 844 both name Murugan or Siva as guru at this shrine.

843.reading: The poet pictures the body as a house of earth and water built of blood, fat, marrow, bone, flesh, guts and nerves, which the soul enters and lives in, flown off with deceit and the greed for wealth like a bird, then struck by fever, bile and winds, its strength shrinking until it goes on a stick, bent like the monkey clan, and asks whether, afraid when it finally slips, he will simply become a corpse. The praise, in drum syllables, shows the vel that scattered Sura and the hill, the gods bowing until their head-garlands scent the golden feet, and names Murugan the guru who gave the discourse of wisdom to his father, guru of the world, at Tirupperunthurai.
843.nuance: மண்சல வீடு, a house of earth and water, makes the body a hut built of the elements; பொருளாசை எனும் புள் makes greed a bird that carries the soul off. சடமாமோ, 'shall I become a corpse?', ends the plea as a question rather than a prayer. செகத்தினின் குருவாகிய தந்தைக்கு அளித்திடும் குரு ஞானப் ப்ரசங்க: Murugan as guru to Siva, the world's guru.

844.reading: The poet speaks of women with kumkum-painted breasts whose bangled arms embrace and whose fish eyes roll in delight until understanding is lost, and asks whether Murugan will now be willing to give his holy feet so that he may cross the great sea of birth. The praise names the vel that burned the hill and the demons' city, Vishnu who held Mandara in the sea, and the four-faced Brahma who worship the feet, and Sankara who sits as guru under the holy kurunda tree, with whom Murugan dwells at Tirupperunthurai.
844.nuance: திருக்குருந்தடி அமர் குருத்வ சங்கரர்: Siva seated as guru under the kurunda tree at Perunthurai, the scene of Siva's teaching of Manikkavasagar there, though the song does not name the saint. Here the guru is Siva and Murugan dwells with him, a reversal of the songs where Murugan teaches Siva.

845.reading: The poet describes a night of lovemaking in detail, dark hair, poisoned eyes, sweating brow, coral lips, conch bangles crying out, breasts pressed until no space is left between them and life joins life, and asks for grace now so that the memory of that moment and the longing to see those faces leave his heart. The praise tells of Rama, before whom the sea came trembling to worship, who killed the twenty-armed hero and broke Lanka, names Murugan the young one who circles the earth on his peacock faster than thought, at Perunthurai among pearl-bright fields and kurundam shade.
845.nuance: The plea asks not for escape from the women but for the end of the memory (நினைவு நெஞ்சினின்று அற) and of the longing to see their faces (முகமது தெரிசனம் செயும் பரிவற): the trouble is what the mind keeps. உயிர் உயிருடன் உற, life with life, is the poet's own phrase for the union.

links.note: Both list the body's stuff, blood, flesh, fat, bone and marrow; the Tirumanthiram counts it as the perishing adjunct of the soul, while 843 makes it a house of earth and water the soul moves into and must watch rot.

843 pictures the body as a house of earth and water built of blood, marrow, bone, flesh, guts and nerves (எலும்பு ... நாடி புனைந்திட்டு இருக்கும் மண்சல வீடு) that the soul enters. Tirumanthiram 461 says the Lord wove bones, bound them with nerves and made a house of red flesh (செம்பால் இறைச்சி திருந்த மனைசெய்து) for the seat of life. The same image of the body as a house of bone and nerve serves the Tirumanthiram as wonder at the maker and the song as disgust at its decay.

843 has the soul enter and live in the body's house (வீடு புகுந்திட்டு அதில் மேவி) until it becomes a corpse. Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has not found a home of its own. Both make the body a house the soul only occupies; the Kural's question about a lasting home is the one the song's ending (சடமாமோ) leaves open.

844 asks whether Murugan will now give his holy feet so that the poet may cross the great sea of birth (கருப்பெருங் கடலது கடக்க உன் திருவடிகளைத் தரும்). Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்) and others cannot. The song's plea uses the Kural's image and its condition, the feet, almost word for word.

845 asks for grace so that the memory of a night of union (நினைவு நெஞ்சினின்று அற) and the longing to see those faces leave his heart. Kural 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because even remembering it (உள்ளினும்) gives a joy that does not end. On the reading that both speak of the same remembered union, the Kural prizes the memory as joy and the song asks for it to be erased as bondage.
